## Chapter 1

## Chapter 2

Paris after midsummer lay so still that a conspiracy of silence seemed to have become a crime. From Yokohama to Irkutsk the East was under war conditions; the Viceroy had massed fleet and siege-guns at Port Arthur; Japan had finished her preparations; Manchuria knew every step: Europe would not see. Banks would allow no disturbance; the press said not a word; embassies professed ignorance. The comedy was admirably acted and, for once, Adams knew that the ignorance was assumed. He could not make out how far the Winter Palace itself knew, or how far the Grand Dukes mistook inertia for policy.

He reached Washington on January 6, 1904, and the air changed. For the first time he saw his country think as a world-power. Japanese diplomacy had counted its steps like Euclid; Russian diplomacy did not appear to step at all. Behind the figures, something in the race-weight baffled calculation. The contrast reached point in the White House, where reticence found no favor. Supper at the President’s table became a relief after the European hush. With a vigor of quos ego habitual to his kind, the President said all that he thought of Russian and Japanese, Boer and Briton, and ended outright: war was imminent; it ought to be stopped; it could be stopped—“I could do it myself; I could stop it to-morrow!”—and then gave his reasons for restraint. That he was right, and that, within a generation, his successor would do what he would have liked to do, Adams took for certain; but what fixed itself was the method—the candor and energy that were not inert.

Day by day the war measured force on the historical scale. Japan’s opening was taken as mathematically as a proposition; against any but Russians it might have failed; against them it succeeded; each twenty-four hours offered a new term in a Grammar of new Science. For Adams the value lay chiefly in the political problem nearest home. Hay, who for years had done his work so perfectly that no one knew enough to know it, could not act; the country would have torn him to pieces had he tried. Japan and England saved his “open door” and fought his battle; all that remained was to make the peace, and Adams set his heart on getting it quickly into Hay’s hand. He knew the fall of Port Arthur must lead to negotiation; he felt Hay would inevitably direct it; but the race was close, and while the war swelled, Hay’s strength sank.

Adams obeyed some errands westward and saw what the old formulas could not express. From Pittsburgh through Ohio and Indiana, agriculture gave way to steam; tall chimneys smoked on every horizon; dirty suburbs piled cinders and scrap-iron where farms had been. The new American showed his parentage proudly; he was the child of steam and the brother of the dynamo, already, in less than thirty years, squeezed and welded by power into approach to shape; servant of the powerhouse as the European of the twelfth century had been servant of the Church; the features would follow the parentage.

He crossed again to Normandy in June and found the Virgin’s town-Expositions still open. On the Fête-Dieu the streets of Coutances were altars and flowers; the cathedral was thronged; no Senate could close it on Sunday—or for her. This interested a student of force who had watched modern authority blush for man and his work; the Virgin seemed to own no such scruple. Her power no longer built Expositions one cared to visit; it still could shut them. The force was actual, serious, and, at St. Louis, had been anxiously measured in money. In France it forced even Adams to buy an automobile, which was humiliation enough to prove its reality. He had set aside the summer to study the Virgin, not as a sentiment but as a motive power which had left monuments scattered from Chartres to Amiens. The machine alone could bind them in any reasonable sequence, and though the force that sells sample-cases might seem to have no relation to the force that built cathedrals, the Virgin in the twelfth century would have guided and controlled both bag-man and architect, as she controlled the seeker of history. To his mind it was a problem of mutual attraction as simple as s = gt²/2, if one could but prove it. He needed none for himself; the bills for the automobile sufficed; but a teacher must speak for others. For him she was an adorable mistress who led the automobile and its owner where she would—into those thirteenth-century World’s Fairs that turned Chicago and St. Louis pale; not to her charm or any piety, but to the energy of creation that had flung these fabrics into air.

The automobile’s vitesse best suited to study was a century a minute. The centuries dropped like autumn leaves, and one was not fined for running over them. In the sixteenth, the ocean of worship broke into light dissolved in star-showers; sensuous devotion ran riot; fragments of color flashed in a thousand village windows; remnants of donors knelt with their children in as fresh hues as the day they were burned; still consoled for a paradise paid for and lost. Yet the ONE had become several. Unity counted for more than Three, but the Multiple showed increase. Whether this was progress, and in what direction, the windows did not answer. The Tree of Jesse at Beauvais, with kings in its branches who were hardly edifying sources of divine purity, compared ill with the grave line at Chartres. Complexity, multiplicity, even a step towards anarchy, they suggested; where was the step towards perfection?

Late one midsummer afternoon, wandering Troyes with Thibaut and Joinville for company, he saw men reading a paper in a window. M. de Plehve had been assassinated. Martyrs, murderers, Cæsars, saints, assassins—half in glass and half in telegram—set the head swimming. Was assassination forever to be the last word of progress? The charming church, with its delightful windows and exquisite peace, took sharper expression from the explosive murder. The conservative Christian anarchist had come to his own, but which was he—the murderer or the murdered? The Virgin never looked so winning—so One—as in this scandalous failure of her Grace. To what purpose had she existed if, after nineteen hundred years, the world ran bloodier than when she was born? The stupendous failure of Christianity tortured history. A unity that alternated was no unity; it resolved at last into meaningless motion.

He would not give it up. So long as he could whisper, he would go on as he had begun, refusing to meet his creator with confession that creation had taught him nothing but that the square of the hypothenuse might be convenient. Every man who meant to be effective—even as a machine—had to account to himself for himself and invent a formula for his universe if the standard formulas failed. There education stopped; the formula, once made, could only be verified. Time pressed. The old formulas had failed, and a new one must be made; yet he sought no absolute truth—only a spool strong enough to wind the thread of history without breaking; among indefinite orbits, the one that best satisfied the observed movement of the runaway star Groombridge 1838, commonly called Henry Adams; a common factor for certain definite historical fractions, which any schoolboy could work out if he were allowed to state the problem in his own terms.

Therefore, when fogs and frost stopped his slaughter of centuries, and shut him again into his garret, he sat down, like a boy at school, to shape, after his needs, the values of a dynamic theory.

From these soundings Adams shaped a Dynamic Theory of History: man as a feeble atom captured by the attractive forces of nature, his progress measurable as the assimilation of new energies—from fetish and Cross to compass and gunpowder—each accelerating his orbit toward an unknown perihelion.
